values: Best use: a real document or quote as proof (a page, a letter, a paper), with the quoted words highlighted. Limit: max 30% of runtime. Not for: a page with nothing highlighted or said about it.
Best use: one statistic or contrast that the line says out loud (two or three bars, one hero). Limit: max 6 beats per episode. Not for: numbers the narration doesn't say.
Best use: showing scale (many headlines or pages saying the same thing). Limit: max 3 beats per episode, at most one per act. Not for: a single source.
Best use: the first appearance of a named person or a hero subject. Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: repeating a portrait already shown.
Best use: one small detail inside a crowded picture or page. Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: a picture whose whole frame is the point.
Best use: web pages, specifications or museum records shown as evidence. Limit: max 6 beats per episode. Not for: text the narrator reads in full.
Best use: the turn into each act (chapter number and title). Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: mid-act headings.
Typeface for Archival Desk (LOK-001) headlines and big numbers. Limit: only in episodes using that theme; a typeface, not a picture, so no beat cap.
Typeface for Archival Desk quotes and titles. Limit: only in episodes using that theme; no beat cap.
Typeface for Archival Desk dates, sources and counters. Limit: only in episodes using that theme; no beat cap.
Typeface for Archival Desk body text and UI labels. Limit: only in episodes using that theme; no beat cap.
Best use: the one slow move on a still picture or a held shot (calm limit 3%). Limit: one move per shot; never stacked with another camera move. Not for: diagrams that already move.
Best use: entrances of headlines, labels, charts and underlines. Limit: one entrance per element; no beat cap (it is a motion rule, not a picture).
Best use: brackets, highlights and cards that lock on. Limit: one lock per element; no beat cap.
Best use: only inside HeadlineMatchCut (VIS-003). Limit: follows VIS-003 (max 3 beats per episode).
Best use: the default cut between beats, keeping the focal point within 25% of the screen. Limit: no beat cap (it is the plain cut); use PushThrough or a slate only where they add meaning.
Best use: archive-led episodes (old papers, photos, maps). Limit: the episode's theme, chosen at Gate 0; one theme per episode.
Best use: a light beam or a camera move starting, rising into the next cut, in a pause. Limit: max 6 beats per episode. Not for: under narration words, or every transition.
Best use: one big number or reveal landing, in the pause after the line. Limit: max 4 beats per episode. Not for: ordinary labels.
Best use: a real page or document arriving on screen, in the pause before its line. Limit: max 10 beats per episode. Not for: text cards or diagrams.
Best use: light-and-colour science episodes (the default for Where Colour Lives). Limit: the episode's theme, chosen at Gate 0; one theme per episode.
Typeface for Warm Graphite (LOK-009) spoken lines, quotes and titles. Limit: only in episodes using that theme; a typeface, not a picture, so no beat cap.
Typeface for Warm Graphite tags, labels, dates and sources. Limit: only in episodes using that theme; no beat cap.
Best use: when the next shot grows out of a key picture in the last one (a detail becomes the next scene). Limit: max 8 beats per episode; never two in a row. Not for: ordinary cuts (use TRN-001).
Best use: the frame layer (grain, grade, vignette) on every beat. This is the one asset meant to be on every frame, because it is the frame itself, not a picture. Limit: none, by design.
Best use: the 20-second 'previously' at the start of each episode, and one return near the end to show which stops are now lit. Limit: max 3 beats per episode. Not for: explaining one idea mid-act.
Best use: a line that names the three cone types, or one that is missing (Young's guess, Dalton's answer, olo). Limit: max 6 beats per episode. Not for: general colour talk with no cones in it.

Best use: where the overlap of the three curves is the point (two lights that look the same, why olo needs a laser). Limit: max 4 beats per episode. Not for: episode 1, before cones are introduced; never as decoration.
Best use: a line that names wavelengths or the band of colours (Newton's spectrum, Dalton's six against his two). Limit: max 5 beats per episode. Not for: background colour or transitions.
Best use: once, right after the cold open. Limit: max 1 beat per episode.
Best use: once, straight after the series title card. Limit: max 1 beat per episode.
Best use: one bed family under narration for the season, chosen with Sam per episode. Limit: drops out under the biggest reveal of each act. Not for: the cold open's first line.
Own (in-house: toolkit media/season_sting.py, option C 'prism'; Sam picked it 22 Nov 2026). No licence or credit needed.
Short opening sting under the series title card, the same in every episode: three soft mallet notes rising low to high (the three cones), then a held fifth; 3.0 s.
Best use: under the series title card only. Limit: max 1 beat per episode.

Mixkit clip 3458 'Candle lighting in the dark' (portrait 1080x1920, 24 fps, 13 s), re-encoded H.264, plus a reversed copy (_rev) so the flame catches at the episode's start. Mixkit Stock Video Free License. https://mixkit.co/free-stock-video/candle-lighting-in-the-dark-3458/
Best use: the candlelit evening in Kendal (episode 1's opening and its return in act 7). Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: any other scene.
Best use: Dalton's geranium (the flower he names in his paper). Limit: max 10 beats per episode. Not for: generic flowers. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0: shown unaltered except grade, credited.
Best use: only as the data inside ConeCurveChart (VIS-013). Limit: follows VIS-013. Not for: hand-drawn curves elsewhere.
Theme: near-black #131313, crimson accent, one lit object at a time, long holds, cut to black. For cold opens and mysteries. Tokens on the Theme_Library tab.

Best use: a whole episode built around one mystery, or a cold open told one lit object at a time. Limit: the episode's theme, chosen at Gate 0; one theme per episode. Not for: episodes carried mostly by documents or data.
Theme: deep teal #15272A, parchment documents and drawn maps, marker red and brass, Libre Caslon. For places and journeys. Tokens on the Theme_Library tab.
Best use: an episode about places and journeys (drawn maps, parchment documents). Limit: the episode's theme, chosen at Gate 0; one theme per episode. Not for: lab or light experiments.
Theme: black #0C0C0C, paper scans on a grid, signal red and steel blue, Inter Tight. For print, design and dye stories. Tokens on the Theme_Library tab.
Best use: an episode about print, design, pigments or dyes, carried by printed pages. Limit: the episode's theme, chosen at Gate 0; one theme per episode. Not for: soft, emotional episodes.

A 3D room or floor drawn as a perspective grid in the theme's hairline colour (one vanishing point, lines fade with depth). Optional objects placed in the same space: a sunbeam, a spectrum on the back wall, a page lying on the floor, a label. One slow dolly per shot (calm limit). For Newton's dark room, Ransome's look-through test, pages on a desk and tilted maps.

Best use: only where 3D space carries the meaning: a light path through a room (Newton's shutter, prism, Experimentum Crucis, lens), a line of sight (Ransome looking through the eye), or places laid out on a tilted map. Limit: max 8 beats per episode; max 8% of runtime; only in acts where the story is in a physical space. Not for: documents (use ArchivalScanCard), comparisons, numbers, titles, or decoration.

Best use: a real clip or photo that sets a scene (a candle in a dark room, a place) with its dateline or label. Limit: max 16 beats per episode; max 15% of runtime (raised from 12 beats, Sam approved at WCL-E01 Gate 1). Not for: documents (ArchivalScanCard) or a named person's first appearance (ParallaxCutout).
Best use: comparing what different people see (by day against by candle; John, his friends, his brother). Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: data with numbers (MinimalDataChart).
Best use: one big span of time said out loud (151 years). Limit: max 2 beats per episode. Not for: dates (DatelineTag) or small numbers.
Best use: lines about the eye itself (Dalton's tinted-jelly idea, the request, Ransome's examination). Limit: max 10 beats per episode. Not for: lines about light or the brain with no eye in them.
Best use: a hinge question or one key label the viewer must keep (WHERE IS THE PINK?). Limit: max 6 beats per episode. Not for: repeating what the narration says word for word, or decoration.
Best use: the first time a new place or date opens a scene. Limit: max 12 beats per episode. Not for: every line with a year in it.
Best use: the candle being lit at the episode's very start (and again only if the story returns to that evening). Limit: max 2 beats per episode. Not for: transitions.
Best use: under the candlelit Kendal scene only. Limit: max 10 beats per episode; max 10% of runtime. Not for: diagrams or documents.
Science History Institute via DPLA / Wikimedia Commons

John Dalton (1798) p. 30: 'sky-blue by day', 'astonishingly changed', 'except my brother'. Public domain. Credit: Science History Institute. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Extraordinary_Facts_Relating_to_the_Vision_of_Colours-_With_Observations_-_DPLA_-_9888a1fc5bcf7520ccdf81a15a0ed40f_(page_26).jpg (Commons page_26 = book p.30)
Best use: the beats where Dalton's own words about the geranium and his brother are quoted. Limit: max 10 beats per episode. Not for: decoration.
Own: Sam's ElevenLabs take (his Samarth voice), paced to 148 wpm with silence only; Sam picked it 22 Nov 2026

Act 1 narration of WCL-E01 'The Man Who Saw Pink' (97.8 s, mono 44.1 kHz WAV; the master of 01_flower_paced_148wpm.mp3). Sam's audio is final: never re-timed, stretched or filtered. Private: Drive only, never GitHub.
Best use: act 1 of WCL-E01 only. Limit: this act's narration, once. Not for: any other act, episode, trailer or Short without Sam's say-so.
Small dots of light travelling along a path, one per ray; inside PerspectiveGrid (kind 'rays') and EyeDiagram section mode. 40 on screen at most.

Best use: only where light physically travels: through Newton's shutter hole, the prism split, the second prism, a lens bringing rays back together, light entering the eye and reaching the back. Limit: max 6 beats per episode; max 5% of runtime; 40 dots on screen at most. Not for: decoration, data or money flows, or any line with no light in it.
Depth haze for the perspective grid (prop fog 0-0.6): far lines and objects fade and soften, a faint haze at the vanishing point, beams scatter wider.

Best use: dark-room perspective-grid shots where depth carries the meaning (Newton's room, Ransome's look-through). Limit: only inside VIS-015 shots; max 8 beats per episode; fog 0.6 at most. Not for: flat shots, documents or titles.

A whole eyeball in three-quarter view as a fine anatomical line drawing on a drafting ground (guide circles, crosshair, ticks); a cut line traces around it on cue, then the front cap lifts away to show the cut face (outer coat, back lining, clear jelly, optional tint); the spoken words sit beside it on their words. Line art only, no blood.

Best use: the request to examine Dalton's eyes and the examination itself (acts 1 and 6). Limit: max 8 beats per episode; max 6% of runtime. Not for: how the eye works in general (EyeDiagram section mode), or any shot that would show real tissue.
Own (studied a Vox-techniques tutorial short by Denys Zhylin; analysis only)
The old shot slides out to the left while the new one slides in from the right (0.7 s, slow-out).

Best use: moving into or out of a document, or between two documents (a scene change, not within a scene). Limit: max 8 beats per episode; never two in a row. Not for: cuts inside one scene (TRN-001) or a detail growing into the next shot (TRN-006).
Own (studied Anton, 'Why Graphic Design Still Matters'; analysis only)
A big letter or number built from small tiles (our own pictograms: cones, rays, eyes, swatches) that assemble on cue.
Best use: act numbers and the numbered keepers at an episode's end; one hero word per episode. Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: body text or labels.
Own (studied Anton, 'Why Graphic Design Still Matters'; analysis only)
The screen fills with thousands of tiny tiles to show a huge number, then collapses to one tile on its word.
Best use: one big-number scale reveal (millions of colours, 1 in 12 men). Limit: max 2 beats per episode. Not for: small numbers (use YearCounter) or decoration.
Own (studied Anton, 'Why Graphic Design Still Matters'; analysis only)
A real picture beside the shape it holds, drawn in tiles or line (a print beside its outline, a spectrum photo beside its curve).
Best use: a real image whose shape carries the point. Limit: max 4 beats per episode. Not for: pictures without a shape to show.
Own (studied Anton, 'Why Graphic Design Still Matters'; analysis only)
Several real sources (pages, prints, photos) laid on a tilted wall the camera glides across, one lit at a time.
Best use: the evidence-pile moment (many papers and reports at once). Limit: max 3 beats per episode. Not for: a single source (ArchivalScanCard).
Own (studied Ben Marriott, 'Best Motion Design of 2026'; analysis only)
A montage of held stills that shows time passing, set against one short burst of motion (stillness against action).
Best use: a long span said out loud (a hundred and fifty-one years), years passing in a life. Limit: max 3 beats per episode; one burst of motion per montage. Not for: comparisons.
Own (studied Anton, 'Why Graphic Design Still Matters'; analysis only)
One key word in a condensed bold face on a solid accent slab, with a tiny mono line under it, locking beside its picture.
Best use: the one word the viewer must keep in a beat. Limit: max 12 beats per episode; never two on screen; only in themes with a condensed face (e.g. LOK-013). Not for: full sentences.
Own (studied Anton, 'Why Graphic Design Still Matters'; analysis only)
A small mono running head top-left naming the current act, on through the act.
Best use: acts longer than 2 minutes, so the viewer always knows where they are. Limit: one per act; off during title cards, quotes and full-frame pictures. Not for: short acts.
Own (studied Anton, 'Why Graphic Design Still Matters'; analysis only)
The ending as numbered keepers (1 to 5): a big numeral and one short imperative line each.
Best use: an episode or season ending that gives the viewer rules to keep. Limit: once per episode, 3-5 items. Not for: recaps of facts.
Own (studied Ben Marriott, 'Best Motion Design of 2026'; analysis only)
A faint chromatic-aberration edge and slow light leaks on top of the grain, adding warmth without taking over.
Best use: candlelit, archival and memory scenes. Limit: max 15% of runtime; never on diagrams or text-heavy beats. Not for: the whole episode.
Own (studied Ben Marriott, 'Best Motion Design of 2026'; analysis only)
The grade flickers gently with a flame in the scene, so the light seems to come from the candle.
Best use: candlelit scenes (Kendal 1792, the 1844 room). Limit: max 12 beats per episode; only where a flame is on screen or just off it. Not for: daylight or diagrams.
Own (studied Ben Marriott, 'Best Motion Design of 2026'; analysis only)
Hand-drawn line boil for our drawn diagrams: the line wobbles a pixel or two every third frame.
Best use: drawn diagrams (eyes, swatches, maps) to feel handmade. Limit: only on line drawings; never on text or photos. Not for: real scans.
Own (studied Ben Marriott, 'Best Motion Design of 2026'; analysis only)
A period engraving-hatch texture for shading the drawings of the 1790s-1840s, set as the drawing's palette rather than a filter on top.
Best use: drawn period scenes (Kendal, Manchester, Ransome's room). Limit: max 10 beats per episode. Not for: modern scenes or photos.
